17039: Ancient Israel lived among peoples who each had their own gods: Baal (Hadad) the storm god and Asherah the mother goddess in Canaan, Dagon among the Philistines, Chemosh in Moab, Milcom in Ammon, Marduk and Nabu in Babylon, and the many gods of Egypt. Most of these were tied to a land, a city or a force of nature, and people worshipped them to secure rain, children, harvests and victory. Israel was drawn to them for practical reasons: Canaan's farms depended on rain rather than a great river, foreign marriages and treaties brought foreign altars, and archaeology shows that many ordinary Israelites mixed the worship of Yahweh with other gods and cult objects. The Bible's writers answer in several ways at once: they tell contest stories in which Israel's God beats a rival on its own ground, they mock idols as wood and metal, they deliberately twist the gods' names into insults, and in later texts they treat the foreign gods as demons. The result is a long argument, running from Exodus to Acts, that Yahweh alone deserves worship and that the gods of the nations cannot save.
17040: Most ancient gods were local and functional: a god of a mountain, a city, the storm, the grain or the sea. Changing land often meant changing gods (1 Sam 26:19; 2 Kgs 17:26).
17041: Baal was the great temptation because Canaan's farming depended on rain, and Baal was the rain god (Deut 11:10-11). The Elijah stories answer him on exactly that ground (1 Kgs 17:1; 1 Kgs 18:41-45).
17042: Archaeology (Ugarit, Kuntillet Ajrud, Khirbet el-Qom, Tel Arad) shows the gods the Bible attacks were real objects of worship, and that some Israelites linked Yahweh with Asherah. How widespread this was is debated.
17043: The Bible often tells 'showdown' stories in which a rival god is humbled on its own turf: the Nile, Dagon's temple, Baal's Mount Carmel, Babylon's procession street (Exod 12:12; 1 Sam 5:3-4; 1 Kgs 18:38; Isa 46:1-2).
17044: Scribes sometimes changed the names of gods and of people named after them, swapping 'Baal' for 'bosheth' (shame) or putting the vowels of 'shame' onto a god's name. If a biblical name looks odd, check the vowels.
17045: Josiah's reform in 621 BC is the Bible's most detailed list of what was actually being worshipped in Judah, from Baal vessels in the temple to horses dedicated to the sun (2 Kgs 23:4-20).
17046: Over time the view of these gods shifted: from rival powers, to lifeless idols, to demons behind the idols (Deut 32:17; Ps 96:5; 1 Cor 10:19-21). Later Christian demonology and Milton's *Paradise Lost* turned the old gods into named devils.
17047: Many popular claims need care: Dagon was probably a grain god, not a fish god; the one-plague-per-Egyptian-god scheme is a later reading; and whether 'Molech' was a god or a kind of sacrifice is still argued.
17048: The plagues and the gods of Egypt
17052: Aaron's staff becomes a serpent; Pharaoh's magicians do the same, but Aaron's swallows theirs. The royal cobra was a symbol of Pharaoh's divine power, so many readers see the first blow aimed at the crown itself.
17055: The river that fed Egypt becomes undrinkable. Traditionally linked to Hapi, the god of the Nile's flood, and to Osiris, whose life-force the flood was said to carry. The text itself names no god here.
17057: Frogs swarm into houses and ovens. Popular teaching links this to Heqet, a frog-headed goddess of birth; she was a minor deity, so the link is suggestive rather than certain.
17059: When the dust becomes gnats, Pharaoh's experts cannot copy it and admit, 'This is the finger of God'. Egypt's own religious professionals concede the contest.
17061: Egypt's herds die while Israel's survive. Often linked to the sacred Apis bull of Memphis and the cow goddess Hathor (traditional pairing, debated).
17063: A darkness 'that can be felt' covers Egypt but not Goshen. Since Ra (Re) and Amun-Ra, the sun gods, stood at the top of Egypt's pantheon, this is the plague most readers connect to a specific god.
17065: Before the last plague Yahweh says, 'against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments'. This is the one place Exodus itself frames the plagues as a contest with gods.
17067: The firstborn die, including Pharaoh's heir. Pharaoh was regarded as a son of the gods and his heir as the next divine king, so the blow lands on the throne's claim to divinity.
17070: Jethro concludes that Yahweh is greater than all gods, and Numbers recalls that on Egypt's gods also Yahweh executed judgments.
17071: Exodus presents the plagues as more than natural disasters: they show who really controls the Nile, the land, the animals, light and life, and they answer Pharaoh's question, 'Who is Yahweh, that I should obey him?' (Exod 5:2). The text explicitly calls this a judgment on Egypt's gods, but it does not match each plague to a named god.
17073: Each plague targets a particular deity: Hapi, Heqet, Apis and Hathor, Ra, and so on. Widely taught since the 19th and 20th centuries and popularised in books such as John J. Davis, *Moses and the Gods of Egypt* (1971). Critics note that Egypt had hundreds of gods, several pairings rely on minor deities, and some plagues (gnats, flies, boils) have no obvious god. Best treated as a traditional, partly speculative reading.
17075: The plagues attack the order (ma'at) that Pharaoh, as divine king, was supposed to uphold. Chaos in river, field and sky shows that Pharaoh cannot keep the world in order, while Israel's God can. This fits Exod 12:12 without needing a god-by-god list.
17077: Some scholars (for example Terence Fretheim) read the plagues as creation running backwards: water, land, animals and light turn against Egypt, echoing Genesis 1, because Pharaoh has opposed the Creator's purposes.
17079: Dates differ (early exodus c. 1446 BC or late exodus c. 1260 BC), and some propose a natural chain of events (red algae, frogs, insects, disease). Others doubt the events are historical in this form. These questions do not change the theological point the text makes.
17083: While Moses is delayed on the mountain, the people ask Aaron to make them gods (or 'a god'; elohim can be either) to go before them.
17085: Aaron collects gold earrings, shapes a young bull, and the people say, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt'.
17087: Aaron builds an altar and announces 'a feast to Yahweh' tomorrow. The people sacrifice, eat, drink and 'rise up to play'.
17089: Yahweh tells Moses the people have corrupted themselves and threatens to consume them; Moses pleads, appealing to God's promise to Abraham, and Yahweh relents.
17091: Moses breaks the tablets, burns the calf, grinds it to powder, scatters it on water and makes the people drink it.
17093: The Levites rally to Moses and kill about three thousand; a plague follows. Moses offers to be blotted out of God's book for the people.
17094: The echo at Bethel and Dan
17095: Centuries later Jeroboam sets up two calves with almost the same words: 'Here are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt'. The writers clearly want readers to connect the two.
17096: The calf breaks the second commandment almost as soon as it is given (Exod 20:4-5). Whether the people meant a new god or an image of Yahweh, the Bible treats making a visible, controllable form of God as betrayal, and later tradition remembers it as Israel's archetypal sin (Ps 106:19-20; Acts 7:41).
17098: Older commentators, Jewish and Christian, often linked the calf to the Apis bull of Egypt, which the people had just left. Bull imagery was common across the Near East, so a direct Apis link is possible but unproven.
17099: An image or pedestal of Yahweh
17100: Because Aaron proclaims a feast 'to Yahweh', many scholars think the calf was meant to represent Israel's own God, or to serve as his throne or mount, as the cherubim did. Bull imagery was used for storm gods such as Baal and for El ('Bull El' at Ugarit). On this view the sin is worshipping the right God the wrong way.
17102: Many critical scholars think the story was shaped (or written) to condemn Jeroboam's calf-shrines, given the identical formula and the plural 'gods' for a single calf. Others reply that Jeroboam was consciously copying an older tradition, so the echo runs the other way.
17104: Paul uses the episode as a warning to Christians tempted by idol feasts in Corinth (1 Cor 10:7), and Stephen cites it to show Israel's pattern of resisting God's messengers (Acts 7:39-41).
17105: Baal-peor: apostasy on the plains of Moab
17106: Shittim, on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan
17108: Camped at Shittim, Israelite men begin 'whoring' with Moabite women, who invite them to the sacrifices of their gods. They eat and bow down.
17111: Israel 'yokes itself' to Baal of Peor, the local lord of Mount Peor. The verb suggests a binding commitment, almost a treaty or marriage.
17113: Yahweh's anger burns; Moses orders the judges to execute those who joined themselves to Baal-peor.
17115: While the people weep at the tent of meeting, an Israelite leader, Zimri, openly brings a Midianite princess, Cozbi, into his tent.
17117: Phinehas the priest spears both of them; the plague stops. Twenty-four thousand have died.
17119: Yahweh gives Phinehas a covenant of lasting priesthood for his zeal.
17121: Later the text blames the episode on Balaam's counsel: unable to curse Israel, he advised luring them into sin.
17122: Deuteronomy, Hosea and the Psalms all recall Peor as a defining failure; Paul cites it to the Corinthians.
17123: On the edge of the promised land, Israel's first open lapse into Canaanite-style worship comes not by force but through hospitality, sex and shared meals. The story warns that the real danger of the other gods lay in ordinary social ties.
17125: Older scholarship often explained Peor as ritual sex in a fertility cult. The text links sex and sacrifice, but evidence for organised 'sacred prostitution' in Canaan is now widely doubted, so many scholars treat this as an over-reading.
17127: Ps 106:28 says Israel 'ate the sacrifices of the dead'. Some scholars connect Peor with the marzeah, a feast associated with the dead known from Ugarit and later texts, and read Baal-peor as having an underworld side.
17129: The language of being 'yoked' and the Midianite princess suggest alliance politics as well as religion: joining Moab and Midian meant joining their god.
17131: Paul says 23,000 fell 'in one day' (1 Cor 10:8). Suggested explanations: he is quoting from memory, combining with Exod 32, rounding, or counting only those who died in a single day. It is a well-known small discrepancy.
17135: Israel loses the battle of Ebenezer; the ark is captured and Eli's sons are killed. Eli's daughter-in-law names her son Ichabod, 'the glory has departed'.
17137: The Philistines set the ark beside Dagon in his temple at Ashdod, as conquerors did with the gods of defeated peoples.
17139: Next morning Dagon has fallen on his face before the ark, the posture of a worshipper. They put him back.
17141: The next morning he has fallen again, with head and hands cut off on the threshold; 'only Dagon was left' (the Hebrew is odd, probably 'only his trunk').
17143: This is given as the reason Dagon's priests do not step on the threshold at Ashdod. Zephaniah later condemns those who 'leap over the threshold', perhaps the same custom.
17145: Yahweh's hand strikes Ashdod with tumours ('ophalim'). The ark is passed to Gath and then Ekron, and panic follows it.
17147: The Philistine priests and diviners advise sending it back with a guilt offering: five golden tumours and five golden mice, one for each Philistine ruler, and to 'give glory to the God of Israel'. They recall Egypt's hardness of heart.
17149: Two nursing cows pull the cart straight to Beth-shemesh, against their instinct, confirming it was Yahweh's doing.
17150: Israel's God has not been defeated with his people. In the enemy god's own house he humbles the rival, who ends up bowing and broken. The point is that the ark's capture was judgment on Israel, not proof that Dagon was stronger.
17151: Dagon the grain god, not a fish god
17152: The 'fish god' idea comes from Hebrew dag (fish) and medieval Jewish commentators such as Rashi and David Kimchi. Most scholars now connect Dagon (Dagan) with dagan, 'grain'. He was worshipped far earlier at Ebla and Mari (3rd millennium BC) as a great lord of the land, and Ugaritic texts call Baal 'son of Dagan'. The Philistines, newcomers from the Aegean, seem to have adopted him locally.
17154: 'Ophalim' means swellings or mounds. The KJV's 'emerods' (haemorrhoids) follows Jewish tradition; the Masoretes even marked a politer word (techorim) to be read aloud. Because mice are mentioned, many suggest bubonic plague with swollen lymph nodes; others doubt plague bacteria were present in the region then. The cause is uncertain.
17156: Carrying off a defeated people's gods was standard Near Eastern practice (Assyrian kings boast of it). The story turns this custom upside down: the captured God punishes his captors.
17158: Many scholars think 1 Sam 4-6 (with 2 Sam 6) was once a separate 'Ark Narrative', perhaps written to explain the ark's absence and return. This affects how they date the story, not its theological point.
17159: Samson in the temple of Dagon
17162: Betrayed by Delilah, Samson is blinded, bound in bronze and set to grind grain in the prison at Gaza.
17164: A quiet note: his hair begins to grow again.
17166: The Philistine lords gather for a great sacrifice to Dagon, singing that their god has given their enemy into their hands. The people praise their god when they see Samson.
17168: Samson is brought out to entertain them and placed between the pillars; about three thousand watch from the roof.
17170: He asks Yahweh to remember him and strengthen him once more to avenge his two eyes.
17172: Pushing the two central pillars, he brings the house down; he kills more in his death than in his life.
17174: His family recover his body and bury him; he had judged Israel twenty years.
17175: The Philistines credit Dagon with Samson's capture, so the collapse of Dagon's house is a public reversal: the feast to Dagon becomes the occasion of Yahweh's victory through a broken man.
17177: Philistine temples excavated at Tell Qasile (by Amihai Mazar) and Tel Miqne-Ekron had roofs supported by two central pillars set close together, which makes the story's architecture believable.
17179: Hebrews lists Samson among those who 'out of weakness were made strong' (Heb 11:32-34). Many Christian and Jewish readers see his final prayer as genuine repentance.
17181: Others note that Samson's prayer is for personal revenge and that Judges presents him as a flawed, self-destructive judge, a sign of how far Israel had fallen; the victory is God's in spite of him.
17182: Elijah and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel
17185: Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians, and builds a temple for Baal in Samaria. Elijah announces that no dew or rain will fall except by his word: a direct challenge to the rain god.
17187: Elijah summons 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah 'who eat at Jezebel's table' and asks the people how long they will limp between two opinions.
17189: They call on Baal from morning to noon and limp around their altar, but there is no voice and no answer.
17191: Elijah taunts them: perhaps Baal is musing, or has 'gone aside' (probably a crude joke about relieving himself), or is travelling, or asleep. Ugaritic myths do show Baal away, dead or sleeping.
17193: They shout louder and gash themselves with swords and lances until blood flows, and rave until evening. Self-cutting was a mourning rite in the region (forbidden in Deut 14:1) and may have been a plea to a god thought dead.
17195: Elijah repairs Yahweh's altar with twelve stones for the tribes and has it drenched with water three times, so no trick is possible.
17197: After a short prayer, fire falls and consumes sacrifice, wood, stones and water. The people cry, 'Yahweh, he is God'.
17199: Elijah has the prophets of Baal seized and killed at the brook Kishon.
17201: Elijah prays on the summit; a small cloud rises from the sea and a great rainstorm follows.
17202: The contest is fought on Baal's own terms: fire (lightning) and rain were the storm god's speciality. Yahweh sends both, and Baal sends neither. The story's question is not which god is stronger in general but which god actually gives Israel its rain and life.
17204: Most scholars read the narrative as a deliberate polemic: Baal 'rider of the clouds' with thunderbolt in hand is shown to be silent, and Yahweh takes over his roles (compare Ps 29). Carmel, on the border with Phoenicia, was a fitting stage.
17206: Jezebel's god is often identified with Baal-Shamem or Melqart, the god of Tyre, rather than Hadad of Ugarit. The text simply says 'Baal'; scholars are divided.
17208: Some historians see the story as legend shaped by later conflicts over Baal worship; others accept a historical core. Everyone agrees the narrative is carefully crafted, with its repeated threes and twelves.
17210: The killing of the prophets follows Deuteronomy's law on false prophets (Deut 13:1-5). Jewish and Christian readers have long wrestled with it; Jesus rebukes disciples who want to copy Elijah's fire (Luke 9:54-55), and James uses Elijah instead as a model of prayer (Jas 5:17-18).
17212: Samaria, with messengers bound for Ekron
17214: King Ahaziah of Israel, Ahab's son, falls through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and is badly hurt.
17216: He sends messengers to ask Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether he will recover. Ekron's god evidently had a reputation as an oracle for healing.
17218: The angel of Yahweh sends Elijah to intercept them: is it because there is no God in Israel that you go to Ekron? The king will die.
17220: The messengers turn back and describe a hairy man with a leather belt; Ahaziah knows it is Elijah.
17221: Two captains with fifty men each are sent to arrest Elijah; fire falls from heaven and consumes them.
17223: The third captain kneels and begs for his men's lives; Elijah goes with him to the king.
17225: Elijah repeats the verdict to Ahaziah's face, and the king dies, leaving no son.
17226: Consulting a foreign god for healing is treated as a public denial that Israel's God is present and able. The fire on the soldiers mirrors Carmel: the power Baal was believed to wield belongs to Yahweh.
17228: Most scholars think 'Baal-zebub' (lord of flies) is a scornful twist of 'Baal-zebul' (Baal the Prince), a title of Baal known from Ugarit. The Gospels' 'Beelzebul' preserves the original form.
17230: A minority hold that the god really was invoked as lord over flies, averting disease-bearing insects, comparable to Greek titles like Zeus Apomyios. On this view the name is not a pun.
17232: Readers have long been troubled by the deaths of a hundred soldiers. Jesus refuses to repeat the act when James and John want to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54-55), which many Christians take as a deliberate contrast.
17233: Mesha of Moab, Chemosh and the sacrifice on the wall
17236: Mesha king of Moab, a sheep breeder, pays Israel a huge tribute in lambs and wool; after Ahab's death he rebels.
17238: On his own stone monument (the Mesha Stele) Mesha says Omri oppressed Moab 'because Chemosh was angry with his land', and that Chemosh then told him to take Nebo from Israel. He claims victory and that 'Israel has perished for ever'.
17240: Jehoram of Israel, Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom march around the south of the Dead Sea and run out of water.
17242: Elisha, playing on a minstrel's music, predicts water without rain; ditches fill, and in the morning sun the water looks like blood to the Moabites.
17244: Israel routs Moab, ruins its cities, stops its wells and fells its good trees, and besieges Kir-hareseth.
17246: Failing to break out, Mesha offers his eldest son, the crown prince, as a burnt offering on the city wall.
17248: 'There was great wrath against Israel', and they withdraw to their own land. The text does not say whose wrath.
17249: This is one of the rare cases where we have both sides. The Bible and the Mesha Stele use the same theology in mirror image: a nation's god is angry with his land and lets the enemy oppress it, then turns and gives victory. The puzzling ending of 2 Kings 3 has made this one of the most discussed verses about foreign gods.
17251: Some scholars read the 'wrath' as the anger of Chemosh, roused by the sacrifice. On this view the writer concedes, at least as narrative, that Moab's god acted on his own ground, reflecting the older idea of territorial gods.
17253: Others think the wrath is Yahweh's, since in Kings 'wrath' (qetsef) usually comes from God. Israel may be judged for overreaching (felling trees against Deut 20:19-20) or for having driven a king to human sacrifice.
17255: Some translations and commentators (going back to Jewish interpreters) read it as Israel's own revulsion or dismay at the sight, or as Moab's soldiers fighting with renewed fury after their king's sacrifice. Either would explain the retreat without any divine actor.
17257: The two accounts do not describe the same campaign and disagree on timing: Kings dates the revolt after Ahab's death, the Stele within the days of Omri's 'son'. Scholars harmonise this in different ways (for example 'son' meaning descendant) or accept that each side remembered events to its own credit.
17258: Jeremiah and the Queen of Heaven
17261: Years before the exile Jeremiah describes children gathering wood, fathers lighting fires and women kneading dough to make cakes for the Queen of Heaven.
17263: After Jerusalem falls, a group of Judahites flees to Egypt, taking Jeremiah with them.
17265: Jeremiah points to the ruins of Judah as the result of worshipping other gods and warns them not to repeat it in Egypt.
17267: The men and women answer that they will keep burning incense to the Queen of Heaven, as they and their kings did in Judah, when they 'had plenty of food and saw no evil'.
17269: Since they stopped her offerings, they say, they have lacked everything and been consumed by sword and famine. This probably refers to the time after Josiah's reform.
17271: The women add that their cakes 'in her image' and drink offerings were made with their husbands' approval.
17273: Jeremiah answers that this very incense is why disaster came, and gives a sign: Pharaoh Hophra will be handed to his enemies.
